Chapter 7: Facing Barriers — Advocacy, Frustration, and the Fight for Access.
As the days go by, it gets harder and harder to ignore the barriers around us. And I’m not just talking about the obvious physical ones—there are social and systemic hurdles, too. Let’s be honest, the world isn’t always designed with everyone in mind. That realization can sting, can’t it? But here’s what happens for a lot of people: those frustrations turn into fuel. They light a fire, pushing folks to stand up and advocate for change—not just for themselves, but for anyone who faces the same kinds of challenges.
Often, it starts with a single moment. Maybe it’s a locked bathroom door. Or a staircase with no ramp in sight. Or even a brush-off from someone in charge. That surge of anger you feel? It isn’t just about you. It’s about realizing how unnecessary these barriers really are—how easily they could be fixed, if someone would just care enough to make it happen. For some, that moment is the first step into advocacy.
Picture this: one afternoon, a group of friends gathers at a city council meeting. They’re nervous—public speaking isn’t exactly a favorite pastime—but the stakes are just too high to keep quiet. So, they share their stories. Some council members listen with real concern, while others just nod politely. It becomes pretty clear that change isn’t going to happen overnight. But you know what? Every single voice matters.
Advocacy doesn’t always look the same. Sometimes, it’s about writing letters, starting petitions, or joining local disability rights groups. Other times, it’s a quieter kind of action—like teaching a teacher about accessible materials, or helping a local business owner see why a ramp really matters. There are big wins—like the excitement when a new elevator finally gets installed—and setbacks, when promises get made but not kept.
And yeah, frustration is always there. Some days, the fight feels endless. Progress can seem so slow, measured in inches instead of miles. But there’s also this strong sense of solidarity. You know other people are pushing forward too, and every tiny win is part of something bigger. Over time, advocacy shifts. It becomes less about anger and more about hope—a real belief that an inclusive world is possible, and that everyone has a part to play in making it happen.
Most people don’t see the invisible work that goes into making spaces accessible. It’s a mix of love and necessity, all driven by the conviction that everyone deserves to feel like they belong. The fight for access isn’t over. But with each barrier that comes down, the world gets just a little more open.
